• **Scriptural evidence for the order**
	+ Passages like Romans 8 show the Holy Spirit as the Spirit of Christ and the Spirit of the One who raised Christ from the dead.
	+ St. Peter's testimony that it was the Spirit of Christ through which the prophets spoke (1 Peter 1:11).

• **Distinction within the triune God**
	+ The distinction within the triune God does not negate unity; rather, it affirms the unity.
	+ The Son shares the same divine essence as the Father.
	+ The Holy Spirit's essence is not separate from that of the Father and the Son.

• **Unique expression of the unified essence**
	+ The Father fully resides in the Son, and the Son in the Father (John 14:10).
	+ Each Person reflects their distinct roles.

• **Consensus of the church fathers**
	+ The church fathers refute any differentiation within the Essence among the Persons.
	+ They uphold the unity of the divine essence.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• **The Nature of Christ's Resurrection**
	+ St. Paul's argument in 1 Corinthians 15:16ff relies on the truth that Christ's resurrection guarantees our own
	+ If Christ did not share our nature, his resurrection would be irrelevant to our salvation

• **The Meaning of "The Word was made flesh"**
	+ The phrase does not imply a transformation into flesh or a mingling of substances
	+ It means that the Word assumed a human body, akin to a temple, in which to dwell

• **The Two Natures of Christ**
	+ Christ's divinity and humanity are two distinct natures that remain separate and distinct
	+ However, they are united in one person, with each nature retaining its inherent qualities

• **A Metaphor for the Two Natures**
	+ A person consists of two distinct natures (soul and body) that remain indivisible
	+ This metaphor illustrates how Christ's two natures can coexist harmoniously

• **Scriptural Evidence for the Two Natures**
	+ Scripture alternately attributes qualities that exclusively pertain to humanity, divinity, or both combined natures
	+ This is known as the "communication of properties"

• **Examples of Communication of Properties**
	+ Christ's assertion that He existed before Abraham's creation (John 8:58) is a divine attribute
	+ Phrases like "firstborn of all creation" (Colossians 1:15-17) and "Servant of the Father" (Isaiah 43:10) are also divine attributes

• **Examples of Human Attributes**
	+ Designations like "Servant of the Father" and statements about Christ's growth in age and wisdom (Luke 2:52) are human attributes
	+ Christ's admission of lesser knowledge than the Father's (Matthew 24:36) and His limited awareness of the final day (John 3:13) are also human attributes

• **The Concept of Communication of Characteristics**
	+ This concept is discerned in St. Paul's assertion that "God obtained His church by His blood" (Acts 20:28)
	+ It refers to the way Christ's humanity and divinity are united in one person, with each nature retaining its inherent qualities

• **Passages that Illustrate the Unity of Christ's Two Natures**
	+ The Gospel of St. John contains many passages that illustrate the unity of Christ's two natures
	+ These passages demonstrate Christ's authority to forgive sins, raise the dead, grant righteousness, holiness, and salvation

• **The Importance of Understanding Christ's Essence**
	+ To truly grasp Christ's essence, we must explore passages where both natures are united
	+ This requires a deep understanding of the communication of properties and the unity of Christ's two natures.

	+ It does not insinuate God's wrath toward Christ, but rather His experience of divine punishment

• **God's Law and Forgiveness**
	+ God's law prescribes offerings for voluntary and unwitting sins (Leviticus 6:2ff, 4:2, 13, 22, 27)
	+ Christ's singular sacrifice has the potency to forgive intentional sins of the faithful

• **David's Case**
	+ David's knowledge of the law and his condemnation of adultery and homicide make it unlikely he was ignorant of their gravity
	+ David's actions demonstrate that even those who know the law can still sin intentionally

• **Patriarchs and Corinthians**
	+ The patriarchs and Corinthians received instruction in the law, yet still committed immorality and other sins
	+ This shows that even those who know the law can still sin intentionally

• **Peter's Denial**
	+ Peter's denial of Christ demonstrates that even those who have received instruction can still sin intentionally
	+ Peter's actions show that he knew what he was doing was wrong

• **Early Church Scholars**
	+ Early church scholars interpreted daily forgiven sins as minor transgressions arising from frailty
	+ They believed that solemn penance was required for serious offenses, but not repeated

• **Interpretation of Scripture**
	+ Scripture demands a more tempered and compassionate approach to forgiveness
	+ The strictness of ecclesiastical discipline should not plunge the beneficiaries of correction into abject sorrow

• **Apostle's Authority**
	+ The apostle's words in Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26-27 are often cited as evidence against forgiveness of voluntary sins
	+ However, these passages must be interpreted in relation to the sin against the Holy Spirit

• **The Sin Against the Holy Spirit**
	+ The sin against the Holy Spirit is the only sin that cannot be forgiven (Matthew 12:31-32, Mark 3:28-29, Luke 12:10)
	+ The apostle's words in Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26-27 refer to this sin, not intentional sins of the faithful

• **Novatianism**
	+ The Novatians misinterpreted the apostle's words to deny forgiveness of voluntary sins
	+ This led to a disturbance in the church, but the apostle's words do not support this interpretation

• **Conclusion**
	+ Christ's singular sacrifice has the potency to forgive intentional sins of the faithful
	+ The apostle's words in Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26-27 refer to the sin against the Holy Spirit, not intentional sins of the faithful.

• **Definition of the Unpardonable Sin**
	+ According to St. Augustine, it is an unyielding, persistent obstinacy up until death, coupled with a lack of trust in obtaining grace.
	+ However, this interpretation does not align with Christ's statement that it will not be forgiven in this age.

	+ Christ says it will not be forgiven in this age or in the age to come (Matthew 12:32).
	+ This statement leaves two options: either it is superfluous or it can be committed in this present world.

• **St. Augustine's Interpretation**
	+ According to St. Augustine, the unpardonable sin is only committed if one perseveres in it until death.
	+ However, this interpretation is not supported by solid evidence.

• **Sin Against the Holy Spirit**
	+ I posit that one sins against the Holy Spirit when they obstinately resist God's truth for the sake of resistance itself.
	+ This is despite being touched by the light of God's truth and unable to claim ignorance.

• **Blasphemy Against the Spirit**
	+ Speaking against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come (Matthew 12:32).
	+ This can include insulting the Son of God, which indirectly affronts His Spirit.

	+ Those who reject and scorn the gospel's teachings, despite recognizing their divine origin, commit blasphemy against the Spirit.
	+ This includes individuals who attempt to thwart God's teachings and undermine His glory.

	+ The spirit of blasphemy manifests when a deliberate malevolence endeavors to undermine God's glory.
	+ This can include individuals who knowingly and willfully renounce Jesus Christ.

• **Deliberate Unbelief**
	+ Deliberate unbelief stemming from knowledge and malevolence must logically be bereft of mercy.
	+ This is in contrast to ignorance and unbelief prompted by negligence, which can receive absolution.

• **The Novatians' Misconstrued Terms**
	+ The Novatians and their adherents misconstrued the terms "fall" or "overturn" to suggest that one stumbles by failing to adhere to God's law.
	+ However, this interpretation is not supported by the biblical context.

	+ This includes individuals who distance themselves from His Spirit and reject His teachings.

	+ Characterized by a deep sense of shame, wretchedness, and hope for transformation

	+ Some perceive two distinct forms of repentance: "legal" and "evangelical"
	+ Legal repentance is characterized by a focus on divine retribution and judgment, leading to ruin and perdition

	+ Cain, Saul, and Judas are examples of individuals who exhibited legal repentance

• **Examples of Evangelical Repentance**
	+ Hezekiah is an example of an individual who exhibited evangelical repentance
	+ Despite being pierced by the sting of sin, he rose with confidence in God's mercy and returned to Him

• **Key Differences**
	+ Legal repentance is characterized by a focus on judgment and retribution, while evangelical repentance is characterized by a focus on God's mercy and benevolence

• **Conclusion**
	+ True repentance involves recognizing one's belonging to God and comprehending His boundless grace
	+ Evangelical repentance is the only form of repentance that leads to transformation and salvation.

	+ Three causes contribute to making our works pleasing to God:
		- The Lord envelops and embraces our works in His Christ through faith alone.
		- His benevolence and paternal munificence bestow value and regard upon our works, irrespective of their worthiness.
		- He accepts our works in His mercy, overlooking their inherent imperfections.

	+ The sophists at Sorbonne err in asserting that works are not deemed worthy of meriting salvation due to their internal goodness.

	+ Some argue that if God wanted to, He could prevent the evils He foresees.
	+ They claim that it appears God intentionally creates people in such a way that they would behave as they do.

• **Addressing the difficulty**
	+ We must accept what Solomon tells us: God created everything for Himself, even the wicked for the day of their destruction.
	+ God arranges and ordains by His plan that some are indeed destined for eternal damnation from the moment of their birth.

• **The perspective that God does not impose necessity through His providence**
	+ Some argue that God sees how wicked people are and creates them for such a condition.
	+ However, this perspective is incomplete and may not fully address the objection.

Here are 10 bullets with sub-bullets summarizing the text:

• **God's Foreknowledge and Will**
	+ God's foreknowledge is not the cause of everything, but rather a result of His will.
	+ God's will is the necessity behind all things, and what He has ordained and willed must inevitably occur.

• **Laurentius Valla's Distinction**
	+ Valla argues that life and death result from God's will rather than His foreknowledge.
	+ God's foreknowledge is a result of His determination of future events, not a cause of them.

• **God's Providence**
	+ God's providence is the legitimate target of criticism, not His foreknowledge.
	+ God's providence is His plan and arrangement for all things.

	+ God foresaw the fall of the first man and the subsequent destruction of all his descendants.
	+ God willed the fall of man, not just permitted it.

• **God's Permission vs. Will**
	+ Some argue that the wicked perish because God permits it, not because He wills it.
	+ However, God's permission implies His will, and it is unreasonable to think that God did not ordain the conditions for the fate of His creatures.

• **Predestination and Necessity**
	+ Predestination is the arrangement and dispensation of divine righteousness.

	+ The cause of damnation is not God's predestination, but rather the corrupt nature of people.

• **The Role of Human Vices**
	+ Human vices, such as turning away from God, are the evident cause of damnation.
	+ The fall of man was a result of his own vices, not God's will.

• **God's Glory and Righteousness**
	+ When we speak of God's glory, we must also consider His righteousness.
	+ God's righteousness is equitable and deserves praise.

• **The Incomprehensibility of God's Predestination**
	+ God's predestination is hidden and utterly incomprehensible.
	+ We should not be disturbed by submitting our minds to God's infinite wisdom.
